description: MIVA ORION is a five member innovation team from Miva Open University, participating in the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026. We are passionate about science, technology, data exploration and understanding Earth's changing systems. Through research, creativity and collaboration, we aim to transform complex Earth observation data into meaningful insights. Our team brings together diverse perspectives, curiosity and a shared commitment to innovation.
summary:
Ground Truth is a free web platform that tells real Earth trends apart from noise. Built for Africa and open to the whole planet, it lets anyone ask a question by voice or text, such as "Is Lagos losing its green spaces?" Our AI analyst, Aisha, flies a 3D globe to the place and checks five long-term NASA records: GISTEMP temperature, MODIS vegetation, GPM IMERG rainfall, GRACE/GRACE-FO water storage and GLDAS groundwater. Live fires come from FIRMS, and this month against normal from NASA POWER.

This addresses the challenge directly. For each place, Ground Truth determines what is changing, where, by how much, and whether it is statistically significant. It uses a Mann-Kendall test corrected for autocorrelation, Theil-Sen slopes with 95% ranges, and false-discovery control across the map. Every claim is labelled Proven, Not proven yet or Observed, with its chart, source and downloadable data. We validated it against six published findings, and it reproduces all six.

This matters because one unusual year often gets reported as a trend, and Africa has the least ground data to check claims against. Ground Truth puts decades of NASA evidence in plain words, on any phone.
details:
What it does
Ground Truth is a free web platform that tells real Earth trends apart from noise. Anyone can ask a question by voice or text, such as "Is drought killing the plants around Abuja?" Our AI analyst, Aisha, flies a 3D globe to the place and tests five long-term NASA records and models:

  • temperature (GISTEMP v4, 1980–2025)
  • plant greenness (MODIS Terra, 2001–2025)
  • rainfall (GPM IMERG, 2001–2024)
  • water stored in the land (GRACE/GRACE-FO, 2003–2023)
  • groundwater (GLDAS-2.2, 2003–2025)

She adds live fires (FIRMS) and this month compared with normal (NASA POWER). Every claim is labelled "Confirmed trend", "Not confirmed yet", "Observed" or "Possible explanation", with a chart, the source, caveats and a CSV download. Every number she speaks is checked against the data before it is shown.

How it works

  • We turn each record into yearly maps with Google Earth Engine and NASA APIs.
  • We test every grid cell (481,199 tests across the five layers) with a Mann-Kendall trend test corrected for autocorrelation, a Theil-Sen slope with a 95% range, and false-discovery control across the whole map.
  • Aisha uses 9 data tools and builds evidence cards from the raw results.
  • We spot-checked the method against published science, and it reproduces 6 of 6 known findings, such as Arctic warming at 3.3× the global rate and north-west India's groundwater loss.

Benefits and impact
One unusual year often gets reported as a trend, and Africa has the least ground data to check claims against. Ground Truth puts decades of NASA evidence in plain words, on any phone. Example: a journalist checking "drought is killing Abuja's vegetation" learns that the heat and the browning are confirmed trends, but the rainfall decline is not confirmed. So the drought claim can't be supported, and urban growth is a plausible alternative. It's built first for journalists, then students, researchers, policymakers and educators. It starts with Africa and works anywhere on Earth.

Tools

  • Python, FastAPI, NumPy, SciPy, pyMannKendall, xarray and the Earth Engine API
  • React, TypeScript, Vite, Tailwind, CesiumJS, GSAP and Motion
  • OpenAI models for text and realtime voice
  • Hosted on Railway

Creativity

  • Talking to an AI analyst who will only call a change real after a statistical test.
  • Honest "not confirmed yet" verdicts instead of guesses.
  • A Lite mode that switches on by itself on slow African mobile networks.

What we considered

  • Honest limits, stated on every result: grids of 55–220 km, temperature interpolated where stations are sparse, and the groundwater trend is a model.
  • Low bandwidth: Lite mode keeps it usable on slow networks.
  • Clear credits for all data and tools.
